title: AQA GCSE Chemistry · Carbon Structures and Nanoparticles

items.stem: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and with what?

options.text: Four covalent bonds, with four other carbon atoms
Four covalent bonds, to atoms of other elements
Four covalent bonds, inside a small molecule
Three covalent bonds, to other carbon atoms

items.why: The specification states that in diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.

items.stem: Which set of properties does diamond have?

options.text: Very hard, low melting point, does not conduct
Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct
Very hard, very high melting point, conducts electricity
Soft and slippery, high melting point, conducts

items.why: These are exactly the three properties of diamond given by the specification.

items.stem: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.

options.text: The weak forces between diamond's molecules must be overcome
The delocalised electrons hold the carbon atoms in place
Many strong covalent bonds have to be broken to melt it
Its carbon molecules are heavy, so more energy is used

items.why: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking very many strong covalent bonds.

items.stem: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.

options.text: Covalent bonds between its layers stop electrons moving
Its delocalised electrons cannot move through the structure
It has no ions, and only ions can carry a current in a solid
All four outer electrons of each carbon are in bonds

items.why: With every outer electron used in a covalent bond, diamond has no delocalised electrons to carry charge.

items.stem: In graphite, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to, and how are the atoms arranged?

options.text: Four others, in layers built from rings of six atoms
Three others, in layers built from rings of six carbon atoms
Three others, in a giant three-dimensional network
Three others, in rings of five joined into a hollow ball

items.why: The specification states three covalent bonds per carbon atom, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

items.stem: What does the specification say about bonding between the layers in graphite?

options.text: Strong covalent bonds join each layer to the next
The delocalised electrons form covalent bonds between layers
There are no covalent bonds between graphite's layers
Each layer shares pairs of electrons with the next

items.why: The specification says the layers of hexagonal rings have no covalent bonds between the layers.

items.stem: How many electrons from each carbon atom in graphite are delocalised?

options.text: All four of the outer electrons of every carbon atom
Two electrons from each atom, leaving 2+ ions in the sea
None: every electron in graphite is in a bond
One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised

items.why: The specification states that in graphite one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.

items.stem: Explain why graphite is soft enough to leave a mark on paper.

options.text: Layers slide off because no covalent bonds join them
Its covalent bonds are weak, so the structure crumbles
Its delocalised electrons let the carbon atoms slide past
Graphite melts at a low temperature and rubs away easily

items.why: With no covalent bonds between the layers, whole layers slide over one another and rub off.

items.stem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity.

options.text: Its carbon atoms move along the layers carrying charge
Ions in graphite are free to move between the layers
One delocalised electron per carbon atom can move through it
Each carbon has a spare electron held in a covalent bond

items.why: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, and delocalised electrons are free to move.

items.stem: In what way is graphite similar to a metal?

options.text: It can be hammered into new shapes without breaking
It is held together by strong ionic bonds, as metals are
It is built from positive ions in a sea of electrons
It contains delocalised electrons that are free to move

items.why: The specification says graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.

items.stem: What is graphene?

options.text: A single layer of graphite, exactly one atom thick
A stack of several graphite layers bonded firmly together
A hollow ball of carbon atoms, like Buckminsterfullerene
A giant carbon structure with four bonds per atom

items.why: The specification defines graphene as a single layer of graphite.

items.stem: Graphene is useful in electronics. Which explanation of this uses graphene's structure and bonding correctly?

options.text: It conducts, because its weak covalent bonds free the electrons
It conducts: each carbon has a delocalised electron
It does not conduct: all four outer electrons are in bonds
It conducts, because it is a hollow cage that traps ions

items.why: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, so one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and free to move.

items.stem: Which statement about Buckminsterfullerene is correct?

options.text: It is a giant covalent structure with the formula C₆₀
It is a solid ball of carbon, with the formula C₆₀
It is a flat sheet of carbon with the formula C₆₀
It is a hollow, spherical molecule with the formula C₆₀

items.why: The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀ ), which has a spherical shape.

items.stem: A structure is described as a hollow cage of carbon atoms built from hexagonal rings together with some rings of five carbon atoms. What is it?

options.text: A fullerene, as its cage can contain rings of five atoms
Graphene, because a graphene sheet is a hollow carbon cage
Diamond, because its rings can hold five carbon atoms
Graphite, because its layers curl into hollow cages

items.why: Fullerenes are hollow molecules based on hexagonal rings that may also contain rings of five or seven carbon atoms.

items.stem: Which description fits a carbon nanotube?

options.text: A solid rod of pure carbon with a very high length to diameter ratio
A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio
A sphere of carbon atoms with a very high length to diameter ratio
A tube of diamond with a very high length to diameter ratio

items.why: The specification describes carbon nanotubes as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.

items.stem: Which of these is a use of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes?

options.text: Cutting and drilling hard rock, as they are the hardest
Lining furnaces, as they melt at a very high temperature
Strengthening composites and use in electronics
Making pencil leads slide smoothly across the paper

items.why: The specification names nanotechnology, electronics and materials as uses of carbon nanotubes.

items.stem: Which particles have diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m?

options.text: Fine particles, which are known as PM2.5
Coarse particles, often called dust
Nanoparticles, which are 1–100 nm wide
Single atoms and simple molecules

items.why: 1 x 10⁻⁷ m to 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m is 100 to 2500 nm, the range the specification gives for fine particles.

items.stem: A particle in smoke is measured and found to have a diameter of 5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Which class of particle is it?

options.text: A nanoparticle, 1 to 100 nm across
A coarse particle, often called dust
A fine particle, only about 5 nm wide
A single atom, about 0.1 nm wide

items.why: 5 x 10⁻⁶ m lies between 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m and 1 x 10⁻⁵ m, the coarse particle range, and coarse particles are often referred to as dust.

items.stem: The side of a cube of a solid is decreased by a factor of 10. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?

options.text: It decreases by a factor of ten
It increases by one hundred times
It increases by a factor of 10
It stays the same, both fall

items.why: The ratio for a cube of side l is 6l² ÷ l³ = 6 ÷ l, so dividing the side by 10 multiplies the ratio by 10.

items.stem: A cube of side 1 cm has a surface area to volume ratio of 6. What is the ratio for a cube of side 0.1 cm?

options.text: 6, unchanged by the cutting up
600, a hundred times bigger than 6
0.6, ten times less than before
60, ten times the first cube

items.why: The ratio is 6 ÷ l, so a side of 0.1 cm gives 6 ÷ 0.1 = 60: as the side falls by 10 the ratio rises by 10.

items.stem: Nanoparticles of a metal can behave differently from a lump of the same metal. Why?

options.text: They are a more reactive element than the metal
They have a much higher surface area to volume ratio
They are built from different atoms than the lump
They each contain fewer than roughly ten atoms

items.why: The specification attributes the different properties to the high surface area to volume ratio of nanoparticles.

items.stem: A sun cream can be made using a metal oxide in bulk form or as nanoparticles of the same oxide. Compared with the bulk form, the mass of the nanoparticle form needed to protect the skin is:

options.text: larger, since each particle is so very tiny
the same, because the oxide is unchanged
smaller, as far more surface gets exposed
larger, as less surface area is exposed

items.why: The specification states that smaller quantities are needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.

items.stem: A typical atom has a diameter of about 0.1 nm. Roughly how many atoms would fit across a structure 1 nm wide?

options.text: About a thousand atoms wide
About one hundred atoms
One atom: 1 nm is one atom
About ten atoms in a row

items.why: 1 nm ÷ 0.1 nm = 10, so a 1 nm structure is only about ten atoms across.

items.stem: A nanoparticle is 20 nm across. A typical atom is about 0.1 nm across. Roughly how many atoms lie along one edge of the nanoparticle?

options.text: About 20 atoms across
About 200 atoms across
About 2000 atoms across
About 20 000 atoms across

items.why: 20 nm ÷ 0.1 nm = 200, so the particle is a few hundred atoms across, as the specification says.

items.stem: Which list gives only applications of nanoparticles named in the specification?

options.text: Fertilisers, road salt, cement, alloys, and water pipes
Research laboratories and specialised university work
Medicine, electronics, sun creams, deodorants, catalysts
Cement, steel making, glass, plastics, and bricks

items.why: These are exactly the applications the specification lists for nanoparticles.

items.stem: A sun cream made with nanoparticles of a metal oxide is clear on the skin and blocks more ultraviolet light than the bulk form, but its long-term effects on skin cells have not yet been fully tested. Which is the best evaluation?

options.text: It should be used, since being on sale proves it is safe
It should be used, because it blocks the most ultraviolet light
There is nothing to pick, as both creams act in the same way
Better protection and appearance, but long-term effects untested

items.why: Uses both sides of the information given and reaches a judgement that names the benefit and the uncertainty.

items.stem: A factory can buy a catalyst as 5 kg of pellets or as 50 g of nanoparticles that speed the reaction just as much. The nanoparticle form costs more per gram. Which evaluation uses this information best?

options.text: Much less mass is needed, so a higher price per gram may pay off
Neither wins, as the reactive nanoparticles wear out fast
Nanoparticles are better, since they are used up faster
The pellets are better, because the nanoparticles cost more per gram

items.why: Weighs the hundredfold smaller mass against the higher unit price, exactly as the information invites.

items.stem: Why do scientists say there are possible risks in using nanoparticles?

options.text: They are on sale already, which proves they are safe
They may enter cells and effects are not known
They are far too small to affect the body's cells
They are used up in reactions, leaving a harmful waste

items.why: Their size lets them reach places larger particles cannot, and the long-term effects have not been fully tested.
